query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace (~0.1 at.%) of boron during the synthesis of CrFeNiTi-based solid‐solution nanoparticles induces in situ precipitation of nanoscale boride phases at internal interfaces, which act as pinning centers that retard grain growth and atomic diffusion, thereby preserving nanoparticle structural and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic CrFeNiTi-based nanoparticles synthesized without boron doping typically exhibit high mobility at grain boundaries and are prone to coarsening and chemical segregation upon exposure to elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Incorporate ~0.1 at.% boron during synthesis (via methods such as mechanical alloying followed by rapid solidification or laser powder-bed fusion) to promote boron segregation and the formation of intergranular boride precipitates.
generation.conditions: Expose both boron-doped and undoped nanoparticles to service-relevant regimes: catalytic conditions at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric conditions at 473–1923 K, including regimes with thermal cycling/annealing to challenge grain boundary integrity.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of finely dispersed boride precipitates at nanoparticle interfaces/grain boundaries that act as pinning centers.
generation.mechanism: During rapid solidification, boron segregates preferentially to nanoparticle interfaces, precipitating as stable borides (e.g., (Hf,Zr)B2-like phases). These precipitates inhibit grain boundary motion and atomic diffusion, thereby limiting grain coarsening and elemental segregation under thermal stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to undoped nanoparticles, the boron-doped nanoparticles are expected to exhibit reduced coarsening, slower rates of elemental segregation, and better retention of functional properties (e.g., catalytic activity and thermoelectric performance) after repeated high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized without boron doping, which are predicted to show more pronounced grain growth, elemental migration, and subsequent degradation of performance upon thermal treatment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to CrFeNiTi-based solid-solution nanoparticles with a controlled low boron level (~0.1 at.%); results may not extrapolate to significantly different compositions or to regimes where excessive boron could form continuous brittle phases.
generation.uncertainty: Although bulk alloy studies support the role of boron-induced intergranular borides in enhancing stability, uncertainties remain regarding the kinetics of boride precipitation and grain boundary behavior in the nanoscale regime, which might differ from bulk analogs.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of CrFeNiTi-based nanoparticles: one doped with ~0.1 at.% boron and one control without boron. Subject both sets to identical thermal cycling and annealing protocols representative of catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) operating conditions.
measurements: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to monitor grain size evolution and precipitate formation.
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) or X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to assess elemental segregation and chemical composition at interfaces.
Measurements of functional properties such as catalytic activity and thermoelectric performance before and after thermal treatment.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped nanoparticles do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in grain growth, elemental segregation, and performance degradation relative to the undoped controls, then the hypothesis that boron-induced intergranular borides enhance high-temperature stability would be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion, the work hardenability and ductility were effectively improved with the addition of boron.Keywords: refractory alloy, high-entropy alloy, boride, grain boundary, mechanical prop

Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.

An equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA was developed in this study, and the addition of a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%, RHEA-B) further overcame the grain-boundary brittleness. As indicated by the microstructural observations and chemical analyses, a simple BCC-phase, solid-solution structure was formed in the matrices of both the alloys. The addition of boron did not obviously increase the hardness of the matrix but induced the intergranular precipitation of the HCP-phase (Hf, Zr)B2 borides which markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Attributable to the lattice distortions caused by the random distribution of different constituent elements, a diminished anisotropy in the mechanical properties was noticed, and the deformation behavior was mediated by many small slips on multiple {110} planes. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion with the addition of boron and the intergranular precipitation of borides, the work hardenability and ductility of the alloy were effectively improved, and the failure mode obviously changed from a mainly intergranular facture to a major portion of the transgranular fracture.

proposals.material_system: MnFeCoNiCu solid‐solution nanoparticles (derived from equiatomic and non‐equiatomic precursor formulations)
proposals.intervention: Synthesize two sets: one with equiatomic composition and one with a tuned non‐equiatomic composition (e.g., reduced Cr content as in MnFeCoNiCu) via controlled cooling from the melt (~4 °C/h over several days) to target enhanced chemical uniformity.
proposals.conditions: Expose both nanoparticle sets to catalytic operating temperatures (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric testing conditions (473–1923 K) under inert and mildly oxidizing atmospheres.
proposals.structural_mediator: Local chemical ordering and fluctuations in elemental distribution that dictate phase stability.
proposals.mechanism: Optimized non‐equiatomic compositions are hypothesized to exhibit smaller fluctuations in local chemical potentials, thereby suppressing elemental segregation and phase separation under high-temperature exposure. The reduced concentration of elements prone to oxidation or diffusion (e.g., Cr) stabilizes the homogeneous solid-solution.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The non‐equiatomic nanoparticles will display fewer chemical and structural changes (lower segregation, reduced precipitate formation) after thermal exposure relative to the equiatomic baseline, verified by techniques such as in situ XRD and X-ray absorption spectroscopy.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This study directly tests whether an optimized elemental distribution governs thermal and chemical stability by comparing equiatomic and deliberately tuned non‐equiatomic nanoparticles under service-relevant conditions, thereby linking synthesis conditions to operating stability.

proposals.material_system: PtPdCoCuNi alloy nanoparticles supported on CeO2 nanorods
proposals.intervention: Anchor nanoparticles on CeO2 via hydrogen spillover-driven synthesis to form sub-nanometric clusters with strong metal-support interactions; subsequently subject to controlled thermal cycling.
proposals.conditions: Operate under cyclic oxidative/reductive conditions at 773–1173 K (simulating catalytic environments) and monitor behavior at intermediate temperatures pertinent to thermoelectric applications.
proposals.structural_mediator: Interface bonding between the HEA nanoparticles and the engineered CeO2 support (or similarly defective supports that create anchor sites).
proposals.mechanism: The strong metal-support interaction (possibly enhanced by hydrogen spillover effects) is expected to immobilize the nanoparticles, inhibiting atom migration and coalescence, thus preserving the multielement mixing even under high temperature and redox cycling.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Supported nanoparticles will maintain a narrow size distribution and retain single-phase chemical uniformity much better than unsupported counterparts. In situ spectroscopy and microscopy should reveal less particle sintering and elemental segregation.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By isolating the impact of nanoparticle–support interactions on stability, this approach distinguishes whether external anchoring mechanisms can compensate for inherent nanoparticle mobility and chemical re-ordering at service temperatures.

proposals.material_system: CrFeNiTi-based solid‐solution nanoparticles doped with a trace (~0.1 at.%) of boron
proposals.intervention: Introduce boron during synthesis (e.g., via mechanical alloying followed by rapid solidification or laser powder-bed fusion) to promote the in situ formation of intergranular boride precipitates at nanoparticle boundaries.
proposals.conditions: Test the thermal behavior in catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) service regimes, particularly under conditions that challenge grain boundary integrity (thermal cycling/annealing).
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of nanoscale boride phases at grain boundaries that enhance interfacial cohesion.
proposals.mechanism: Boron segregation leads to the precipitation of fine borides that act as pinning centers at grain boundaries, limiting grain growth and diffusion-driven segregation; this mechanism is anticipated to enhance both mechanical and chemical stability under high temperatures.
proposals.predicted_outcome: B-doped nanoparticles will exhibit reduced coarsening and slower rates of elemental segregation compared to undoped controls, with microhardness and structural continuity maintained after thermal exposure.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach investigates whether engineered interfacial precipitates can govern the nanoscale stability of multi-element systems under harsh conditions, testing a mechanism distinct from intrinsic chemical mixing.

proposals.material_system: PtPdCoCuNi and MnFeCoNiCu HEA nanoparticles with a controlled surface oxidation treatment
proposals.intervention: Perform a mild thermal annealing in a controlled oxygen atmosphere to deliberately form a nanometer-thick, self-limiting oxide skin on the nanoparticles post-synthesis.
proposals.conditions: Subject treated nanoparticles to service-relevant temperatures for catalysis (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric applications (473–1923 K) in both inert and mildly oxidizing environments.
proposals.structural_mediator: A protective oxide shell that acts as a barrier to further oxidation and atomic diffusion.
proposals.mechanism: The formation of a stable, ultrathin oxide layer on the nanoparticle surface curbs further oxidation and inhibits elemental migration, thus preserving the underlying multielement solid-solution structure even under repeated thermal cycling and redox fluctuations.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with the engineered oxide skin will display enhanced resistance to sintering and composition drift relative to untreated nanoparticles, as evidenced by consistent catalytic activity and stable thermoelectric performance over extended high-temperature exposure.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This strategy provides a clear test of whether a deliberately formed surface barrier can control the stability of HEA nanoparticles by preventing structural and chemical degradation in service conditions, offering a direct mechanistic differentiation from bulk compositional approaches.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly addresses the open question by testing whether an engineered interfacial precipitate—in this case, nanoscale boride formed via trace (~0.1 at.%) boron doping—can pin grain boundaries and resist diffusion-driven coarsening and segregation under harsh thermal conditions. Prior evidence (e.g., PMC9572892) in refractory high‐entropy alloys supports that boron addition improves grain boundary cohesion, and adapting this mechanism to CrFeNiTi-based solid‐solution nanoparticles is a clear, testable intervention for catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) applications, especially in systems where low noble-metal content is desired.
